newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Embattled Sao Paulo mayor in tax fraud probe.
newsitem.headline: Embattled Sao Paulo mayor in tax fraud probe.

text.p: Already under fire for his ties to a multi-million-dollar bond scam, Sao Paulo Mayor Celso Pitta is also under investigation for possible tax fraud, a city spokesman said on Monday.
A spokesman for the mayor's office confirmed weekend newspaper reports that Pitta was being investigated by the federal tax agency for allegedly under-reporting his income.
"The Federal Revenue Service is investigating the mayor's income and assets," the spokesman told Reuters in a telephone interview.
"The mayor has said he has nothing to fear. He said he is ready to offer all the necessary explanations," he said.
Pitta, who was sworn into the mayor's office just three months ago, is the focus of a congressional probe investigating a municipal bond fraud in which over $600 million went missing.

Senators leading the investigation say Pitta was at least negligent and may even have cooperated with a group of his direct subordinates who are accused of manipulating bond auctions in order to benefit a handful of small banks.
The auctions took place in 1995 and 1996 when Pitta was Secretary of Finance for the city of Sao Paulo.
Pitta has consistently denied the accusations. Earlier this month he responded by firing four of the City Hall employees accused of masterminding the bond scheme.
As the mayor of Brazil's largest city, Pitta manages the country's third biggest government budget and has considerable influence over politics at a national level.
Over the weekend, national newsweekly Veja cited tax officials investigating Pitta's finances who said the mayor's personal expenditures were in excess of his declared income.
They said Pitta would be called to explain how he recently bought three new cars, a luxury flat and a five-star European tour on his former Secretary of Finance salary of $30,000.
The municipal bond scam is the latest in a long line of Brazilian government corruption scandals that followed the 1992 ouster of President Fernando Collor de Mello.

Collor, who lives in self-imposed exile in Miami, has been cleared of charges of having profited from an influence-peddling ring run by his former campaign manager but is now also under investigation by tax authorities.
